::: {.lesson-hero}
::: {.lesson-kicker}
WEEK 1 · REPRESENTATION, RULES, AND RELATIONSHIPS
:::

# A database is just a glorified spreadsheet.

That claim is useful precisely because it is **almost plausible**. Both tools organize values into rows and columns. Both can sort, filter, calculate, and summarize. So what changes when a table becomes a database?

::: {.lesson-question}
**Guiding question:** Where does a simple file representation of data begin to fall apart—and what capabilities do databases add in response?
:::
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. explain why spreadsheets, CSV files, and relational tables initially look similar;
2. distinguish a **database** from a **database management system**;
3. identify repeated facts, ambiguous identity, and common modification anomalies;
4. explain how keys, constraints, relationships, and transactions address specific failures; and
5. choose a spreadsheet, a collection of files, or a database for a small scenario and defend the choice.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Keep one sentence in mind

A database is valuable not merely because it stores data, but because it can make important **relationships and rules explicit**.
:::

## 1. Why the comparison feels reasonable

Imagine receiving this table from a field team monitoring stream temperature.

| observation_id | site_code | site_name | sensor_model | observed_at | temperature_c |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 8.4 |
| 2 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 10:00 | 9.1 |
| 3 | PR-02 | Pine River | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 7.8 |
| 4 | CC-01 | Clear Creak | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 11:00 | 9.7 |

At first glance, the same information could live in several places:

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### Spreadsheet

A visible grid with formatting, formulas, charts, and direct editing.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### CSV file

A portable text representation of rows and delimited values.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Database table

A named relation managed by software that can query and enforce rules.
:::
:::

They share a familiar tabular surface:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Rows"] --> D["Tabular data"]
    B["Columns"] --> D
    C["Values"] --> D
    D --> E["Spreadsheet"]
    D --> F["CSV file"]
    D --> G["Database table"]

    classDef shared fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d,stroke-width:1.5px;
    classDef tool fill:#ffffff,stroke:#78909c,color:#21313a;
    class A,B,C,D shared;
    class E,F,G tool;
```

This is the source of the “glorified spreadsheet” intuition. The visual shape is similar, and for small tasks the observable behavior may be similar too.

### What all three can do

- Store rectangular data.
- Label fields with column names.
- Select particular rows and columns.
- Sort and aggregate values.
- Exchange data with other tools.

::: {.callout-question appearance="simple"}
## Opening poll

If this file contains only a few hundred measurements and one person maintains it, what problem would a database solve **today**? “None yet” is a legitimate hypothesis.
:::

## 2. Three different things hiding behind one grid

The visual similarity can conceal important distinctions.

::: {.concept-strip}
**Spreadsheet** → a document and interactive calculation environment<br>
**CSV** → a serialization format for values<br>
**Database** → an organized collection of related data<br>
**DBMS** → the software that stores, queries, protects, and coordinates the database
:::

PostgreSQL is a **database management system**. A particular PostgreSQL database contains tables, constraints, indexes, users, and other objects. A CSV is not a lightweight DBMS; it is a file format with very few built-in semantics.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    U["People and applications"] --> Q["Database management system<br/>PostgreSQL"]
    Q --> T1["site"]
    Q --> T2["sensor"]
    Q --> T3["observation"]
    Q --> R["Rules, permissions,<br/>transactions, and indexes"]

    classDef actor fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef system fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    classDef data fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    class U actor;
    class Q system;
    class T1,T2,T3,R data;
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Vocabulary matters

In casual speech we often say “the database rejected the row.” More precisely, the DBMS evaluated the database's declared rules and rejected a change that would violate them.
:::

## 3. Failure point one: the table mixes different kinds of facts

Return to the stream table. Each row records an **observation**, but it also repeats facts about a **site** and a **sensor model**.

::: {.fact-grid}
::: {.fact-card}
### Observation facts

- when the reading occurred
- measured temperature
- which site and sensor were involved
:::

::: {.fact-card}
### Site facts

- site code
- site name
- perhaps location and watershed
:::

::: {.fact-card}
### Sensor facts

- model name
- manufacturer
- perhaps accuracy and serial number
:::
:::

The file stores these facts together because that is convenient for reading a row. Convenience has a cost: `Clear Creek` may be repeated thousands of times.

### Modification anomalies

When one table repeats the same fact, ordinary operations become surprisingly difficult.

| Operation | What can go wrong? | Name commonly given to the problem |
|---|---|---|
| Update a site's name | Only some rows are changed, leaving contradictory names | Update anomaly |
| Add a site before it has observations | An empty or fake observation must be created | Insertion anomaly |
| Delete a site's final observation | The only record of the site disappears too | Deletion anomaly |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Row 4 is not merely a typo

`CC-01` now has two names: **Clear Creek** and **Clear Creak**. The deeper problem is that the file contains no enforceable declaration that one site code identifies one site.
:::

### Checkpoint: locate the repeated facts

For each field below, decide what kind of thing it describes.

| Field | Observation | Site | Sensor | Not enough information |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `observed_at` | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `site_name` | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `sensor_model` | □ | □ | □ | □ |
| `temperature_c` | □ | □ | □ | □ |

What would happen if a sensor model name were corrected after one million observations had been collected?

## 4. Failure point two: identity is implicit

Humans are good at treating labels as identities—until labels change, collide, or are entered inconsistently.

Consider the phrase “the Clear Creek site.” Which field identifies it?

- `site_name` is readable, but names can change and may not be unique.
- `site_code` looks stable, but only if the organization guarantees its meaning.
- the row number identifies an observation, not the site.
- latitude and longitude may drift when coordinates are corrected.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## A key is a claim

Declaring a key is not just a technical maneuver. It asserts that a value—or combination of values—uniquely identifies something in the modeled world.
:::

The choice should follow requirements rather than convenience. Before choosing a key, ask:

1. Can the value change?
2. Can two records legitimately share it?
3. Can it be missing when the record is created?
4. Who controls its meaning?
5. Does it identify the real-world thing or only the current row?

### A database response: separate identity from description

One possible redesign separates sites, sensor models, and observations.

```{mermaid}
erDiagram
    SITE ||--o{ OBSERVATION : "has"
    SENSOR ||--o{ OBSERVATION : "records"

    SITE {
        integer site_id PK
        text site_code UK
        text site_name
    }

    SENSOR {
        integer sensor_id PK
        text model_name
    }

    OBSERVATION {
        integer observation_id PK
        integer site_id FK
        integer sensor_id FK
        timestamp observed_at
        decimal temperature_c
    }
```

This diagram says that each observation refers to one site and one sensor, while a site or sensor may participate in many observations.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple"}
## A diagram is a hypothesis, not an answer key

Do we mean a sensor **model** or an individual physical instrument? Can two sensors record at the same site and time? Can site names change historically? The correct design depends on facts not yet stated.
:::

## 5. Failure point three: relationships become awkward

Rectangular files encourage us to flatten related things into one wide table. This works until the relationships stop being simple.

Suppose one observation can have several quality flags:

- `suspected_ice`
- `sensor_recalibrated`
- `manually_reviewed`

Several spreadsheet-style designs are tempting:

```text
flag_1 | flag_2 | flag_3
```

```text
flags = "suspected_ice; manually_reviewed"
```

```text
suspected_ice | sensor_recalibrated | manually_reviewed
```

Each representation makes some future operations harder. How would we add a new flag type? Prevent misspellings? Attach a reviewer and timestamp to one flag? Find observations with two particular flags?

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    O["One observation"] --> F1["suspected_ice"]
    O --> F2["sensor_recalibrated"]
    O --> F3["manually_reviewed"]
    F1 --> O2["Many observations<br/>can share a flag type"]
    F2 --> O2
    F3 --> O2

    classDef observation fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#fff;
    classDef flag fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    class O,O2 observation;
    class F1,F2,F3 flag;
```

Databases do not eliminate complexity. They give us tools—multiple related tables, keys, and joins—to represent the complexity directly instead of hiding it inside columns or text.

## 6. Failure point four: rules live in people's heads

A spreadsheet can visually suggest rules through color, validation menus, protected cells, or instructions. A CSV cannot even do that. In both cases, another program can often bypass those conventions.

For the stream data, plausible rules include:

- every observation must refer to a known site;
- a site code must be unique;
- an observation must have a timestamp;
- temperature must be within a defensible range;
- two rows must not represent the same observation event.

### From convention to constraint

| Intended rule | Database mechanism |
|---|---|
| Every site has a stable identifier | `PRIMARY KEY` |
| Site codes do not repeat | `UNIQUE` |
| Every observation names a real site | `FOREIGN KEY` |
| Required values cannot disappear | `NOT NULL` |
| Temperature stays in an accepted range | `CHECK` |

Here is a preview of what some of those declarations look like in SQL. You do **not** need to master the syntax today; read it as a set of claims.

```sql
CREATE TABLE site (
    site_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    site_code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    site_name TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE observation (
    observation_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    site_id        INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES site(site_id),
    observed_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    temperature_c  NUMERIC NOT NULL
                   CHECK (temperature_c BETWEEN -5 AND 50),
    UNIQUE (site_id, observed_at)
);
```

::: {.callout-question appearance="simple"}
## Challenge the schema

The database can enforce only the rules we declare, and declared rules can be wrong. Is `UNIQUE (site_id, observed_at)` appropriate if two sensors can operate at the same site simultaneously? What additional information would you need?
:::

## 7. Failure point five: several people act at once

File-based workflows often handle collaboration by creating copies:

```text
observations.csv
observations_jake_edits.csv
observations_FINAL.csv
observations_FINAL_v2_really_final.csv
```

Copies create a coordination problem: which file is authoritative, and how should conflicting changes be reconciled?

Even a shared spreadsheet can expose a more subtle problem when several operations must succeed or fail together. Imagine transferring the responsibility for a sensor from one field team to another.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as "Analyst A"
    participant D as "Shared data"
    participant B as "Analyst B"
    A->>D: Read sensor status = available
    B->>D: Read sensor status = available
    A->>D: Assign sensor to Team North
    B->>D: Assign sensor to Team South
    Note over A,B: Both decisions were reasonable<br/>from the state each analyst saw.
```

A DBMS provides **transactions** and concurrency control so related operations can be treated as a unit and simultaneous work can be coordinated under stated guarantees.

::: {.concept-strip}
**Transaction:** a logical unit of work that should preserve the database's rules even when failures or concurrent actions occur.
:::

We will spend much more time on transactions later. For Week 1, the key idea is that a database is not only a container; it is an active participant in coordinating change.

## 8. Failure point six: questions outgrow the file

Small files are easy to inspect. As data grows, the workload changes:

- combine observations with sites, sensors, maintenance, and weather;
- give different users different access;
- recover after a failed write;
- reproduce a report from a known state;
- find a small subset without scanning everything;
- serve many readers while new observations arrive.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["One table<br/>one person<br/>occasional edits"] --> B["Repeated facts<br/>several entities"]
    B --> C["Many users<br/>concurrent changes"]
    C --> D["Large workloads<br/>security and recovery"]

    A -. "spreadsheet may fit" .-> A
    D -. "DBMS capabilities matter" .-> D

    classDef early fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef middle fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef late fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A early;
    class B,C middle;
    class D late;
```

Performance is part of the story, but “databases are for big data” is incomplete. A tiny database may be worthwhile because the rules matter. A very large immutable dataset may work well in files because it is written once and analyzed in batches.

## 9. Spreadsheets are not failed databases

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Use the simplest tool that preserves what matters

The point is not to replace every spreadsheet. The point is to recognize when a document-oriented grid no longer matches the problem.
:::

### A spreadsheet may be the better choice when…

- one person is exploring or entering a modest amount of data;
- layout, annotation, formulas, and charts are part of the artifact;
- the structure changes frequently;
- the consequence of an inconsistent value is small and visible; or
- the document itself—not a long-lived shared data system—is the product.

### A database becomes attractive when…

- several kinds of things and relationships must be represented;
- identifiers and integrity rules must be reliable;
- many people or applications read and write shared data;
- changes must be atomic, auditable, recoverable, or permission-controlled;
- queries repeatedly combine data in different ways; or
- the data must outlive the spreadsheet layout or original author.

### Decision matrix

| Situation | Spreadsheet | CSV/files | Relational database |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Quick personal exploration | Strong | Moderate | Possible, often unnecessary |
| Portable data interchange | Weak | Strong | Usually exported |
| Rich manual formatting | Strong | None | Not its purpose |
| Enforced relationships | Limited | None | Strong |
| Concurrent structured updates | Limited | Weak | Strong |
| Transactions and recovery | Weak | Weak | Strong |
| Fine-grained permissions | Limited | File-level | Strong |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The boundary is contextual

There is no universal row count at which a spreadsheet “becomes” a database problem. The important questions concern relationships, rules, coordination, risk, and workload—not just size.
:::

## 10. Studio: make the file fail on purpose

Work in groups of two or three. Your goal is not to clean the data immediately. Your goal is to discover what the current representation permits.

### Part A — Observe

Using the four-row stream table:

1. Circle every fact that repeats.
2. Mark the row that creates a contradiction.
3. List three rules a human reader appears to assume.
4. Identify one question the table cannot answer without additional data.

### Part B — Stress the representation

Describe the smallest change that would cause each problem:

- two records appear to identify the same observation;
- one site appears under two names;
- an observation refers to an unknown sensor;
- deleting a reading also deletes the only known fact about a site;
- two people make individually reasonable but mutually incompatible changes.

### Part C — Propose a model

Sketch boxes for the distinct kinds of things you believe exist. Add identifiers and draw relationships. Do not worry about formal ER notation yet.

::: {.studio-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Every box should complete the sentence “This is one _____.” Every line should complete the sentence “One _____ can be related to _____.”
:::

### Part D — Defend one rule

Choose one rule that belongs in the data system rather than only in written instructions. State:

1. the rule in plain language;
2. a minimal example that violates it;
3. why the violation matters; and
4. what database mechanism might enforce it.

## 11. What changed when we moved toward a database?

We did not merely split one file into several smaller files. We added semantics.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["A convenient grid"] --> B["Identify distinct kinds of facts"]
    B --> C["Choose identities"]
    C --> D["Represent relationships"]
    D --> E["Declare rules"]
    E --> F["Coordinate and test changes"]
    F --> G["A defensible data model"]

    classDef start fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef process fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef finish fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A start;
    class B,C,D,E,F process;
    class G finish;
```

::: {.takeaway-panel}
## The revised claim

A relational database may **look** like a collection of spreadsheets, but a DBMS adds a language for declaring identity, relationships, and rules—and machinery for querying, coordinating, protecting, and recovering shared data.
:::

## Exit ticket

Respond in three or four sentences:

> Name one situation in which you would deliberately choose a spreadsheet over a database, and one change in requirements that would make you reconsider. Refer to at least one of these concepts: identity, repetition, relationships, constraints, concurrent work, or recovery.

## Looking ahead

Next, we will learn enough SQL to treat a database not as a static grid but as a system for asking precise questions. We will return to the stream observations and test which claims the database can actually enforce.
